## Prologue: The Geometry of Meaning {#sec-prologue-geometry-meaning .unnumbered}

### Realizing a Word is a Coordinate

There is a distinct moment every engineer remembers when the abstraction behind their tools suddenly dissolves into something far more visceral. For me, that moment arrived while inspecting the internals of a neural language model. Up until then, software had always dealt with words as arbitrary integers or ASCII byte sequences—opaque strings compared with `==` operators or indexed in B-trees.

Looking into the high-dimensional latent layer, however, the text ceased to be strings. Each word, in its context, was represented as a point in a Euclidean space of a thousand or more dimensions: a vector of floating-point numbers $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{D}$. Even more striking was that its location was not random. Words with related meanings occupied tight geometric neighborhoods. Abstract relations mapped to spatial offsets: moving across a specific vector subspace turned verbs from present to past tense, shifted countries to their capitals, or modulated formal language into casual speech. Meaning was no longer an intangible philosophical construct; it was a physical location in a continuous geometric space.

### From Cartesian Coordinates to Latent Worlds

For more than seven decades, computer science operated on a foundational dogma: **information is discrete, and computation is symbolic manipulation over structured records**. 

In 1948, Claude Shannon laid the mathematical bedrock of digital telecommunications by formalizing information as statistical uncertainty reduction, whose simplest form is the entropy of a discrete source:

$$H(X) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x) \log_2 p(x)$$

In doing so, Shannon deliberately set aside the question of *meaning*:

> *"These semantic aspects of communication are irrelevant to the engineering problem."* — Claude Shannon (1948)

More than seven decades later, artificial intelligence has arrived at the reciprocal breakthrough: **the Embedding Revolution**. 

Beneath the architectures of the last decade (attention, diffusion, generative chatbots) lies a profound shift: language, images, molecules, robot trajectories, and relational graphs have all been mapped, with remarkable success, to points in continuous, high-dimensional spaces. Once embedded, similarity becomes an inner product, and analogies often become offsets between vectors.

### What This Book Is

<!-- OPEN: what "revolution" refers to. Candidates: a change in how knowledge is represented (needs a failing predecessor to count as a revolution); one method reaching everything (needs the shared part to be the embedding and not only deep learning plus scale); reasoning as paths in a space; or only a metaphor. Decide after Part II; until then the title is a working title. -->

This is an exploratory book. It has no thesis to defend and no conclusion fixed in advance. Its subject is the spaces, called embedding spaces or latent spaces, in which machine learning places words, images, sounds and other things as points, and what those spaces say about how meaning, discourse, reasoning and thought can be represented. I write it as I explore. Some chapters are settled, some are provisional and some are only questions, and each chapter says which. The plan will change as the evidence comes in, and ideas that do not hold up are dropped.

The question that guides the exploration is whether representing meaning as vectors is a good approach: why it works, what it can express, where it strains, and what each proposed extension, whether curved, topological, quantum, or hyperdimensional, buys and costs. None of those geometries is assumed to be better than the others.

Two ideas run through the exploration. The first is that the mathematics that explains why vectors work (Shannon, Chomsky, Rice, concentration of measure, symmetry, algebra) is far more durable than any model, so each chapter is built around a question of that kind, and tells the methods that explored it as history, with dates. The second is the **bitter lesson** [@sutton2019bitter]: general methods that keep improving as computation grows have repeatedly beaten methods that build in what researchers know. The lesson is about how an algorithm uses computation, not about the shape of the model, and the winner is sometimes linear. Whatever structure is proposed here must align with computational efficiency and scalability, or say why it need not.

The exploration is guided by three things. The first is the classic results of philosophy, mathematics and linguistics, which have outlived every model and say what a representation of meaning would have to be. The second is the way science keeps its hypotheses, by refutation: a claim earns trust by surviving attempts to break it, and the book prefers the test that can show a property is absent to the example that shows it is present (the *via negativa*). The third is experiments small enough for a typical computer, which can be read, rerun and changed by the reader. The aim is insight and a holistic view of the field, and not state-of-the-art performance. A view of the whole may also show gaps in the current approaches, which this book reports as questions and does not promise to fill.

This book is written without a laboratory. It cannot rely on expensive external judgement or on computing power at scale: no panels of human raters, no paid judge models, no clusters. Its own experiments are therefore smoke tests. They can falsify a claim or illustrate a mechanism, and they cannot rank methods at scale. Human judgements come from published benchmarks, and a claim that one method beats another rests on cited comparisons made at scale, with their source and date. Each test of a chapter is posed as a question that a small run can refute, and when it cannot be answered here the book says so and points to the evidence that would.

The direction of the exploration so far is a working frame, not a thesis. Representing meaning as vectors is surprising and it works: Shannon's own quantities (pointwise mutual information, mutual information, cross-entropy) turn into geometry, and carry the book past his exclusion of meaning while the mathematics stays inside his framework. A single vector has limits, and each limit has proposed remedies, each with a price. Two thought experiments probe them, the dog test and the critical literacy test below, and a last part goes beyond the state of the art, starting from what the existing approaches still cannot do and asking what fields outside machine learning have said about the same problem.

### Why Everything is Becoming a Vector

Many kinds of things have been embedded. This book follows the ones that bear on meaning, discourse, reasoning and thought, and mentions the others only as pointers:

- **Natural Language:** Tokens, sentences, and documents mapped to continuous semantic coordinates.
- **Perception (Vision, Audio, Video):** Pixels, audio waveforms, and video frames, each encoded into vectors by encoders built for the symmetries of that signal.
- **Multimodal Meaning:** Text, images, sound, and motion projected into one shared metric space, so that a photograph, a word, and a sound of the same thing become neighbours (e.g., CLIP for images and text in 2021, ImageBind for six modalities in 2023).
- **Biology & Chemistry:** Amino acid sequences and molecular structures represented as continuous vectors (e.g., protein language models).
- **Knowledge Graphs & Logic:** Discrete entities and relational predicates transformed into continuous translational and rotational operators ($\mathbb{R}^D, \mathbb{C}^D$).
- **Action, Planning and Reasoning:** Goals, world states, and plans represented as vectors, and behaviour as trajectories of such vectors (e.g., world models that predict the next state in latent space and plan there). Reasoning can follow such a trajectory too, or keep leaving the space to write each step down in words, as a chain of thought does. Either way it is a draw from a distribution of paths, not a geodesic to the answer: training raises the probability that a path ends in a correct one, and no single path is guaranteed to.

Each item is also a question: what does the vector keep, and what does it lose?

### Embedding Space or Latent Space?

Two names appear in this book for what looks like the same place, and the literature does not keep them apart either. *Embedding space* comes from mathematics and language processing, where an embedding maps objects to vectors so that similar objects are close. *Latent space* comes from statistics and generative models, where a latent variable is the hidden cause of the data. Wikipedia treats them as synonyms, and papers often use both words for the same hidden layer.

What does differ is how a space was trained. A space trained for similarity gives distance a meaning by construction and usually has no way back to the data. A space trained to reconstruct or generate usually has a decoder, and its distances mean only what the training made them mean. This book uses the two words interchangeably, except where the literature has settled on one of them for a context (*latent semantic analysis*, *latent variable*, *latent diffusion*, against *word embedding*, *embedding model*). Where the training matters, it says which kind produced the space. The chapters that build spaces lean on the word their literatures use: *embedding* for the maps of @sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness, *latent* for the generative models of @sec-ch-meaning-as-generation.

### The Dog Test

One question is harder than the others, and it returns throughout this book. Take a dog. There is a photograph of it, the word "dog", the sound of its bark, and a video of how it runs. Four signals with nothing in common at the level of bytes: a grid of pixels, a string of characters, a pressure wave, a sequence of frames. Yet a child who meets a dog through any one of them recognizes the others as the same thing. Firth's company, "you shall know a word by the company it keeps", is a company of words. The dog test asks for more: can a photograph, a word, a bark, and a gait be placed in **one** space, near each other and far from a cat, a car, and a doorbell?

This is the *symbol grounding problem* in geometric form (Harnad, 1990): words defined only by other words never touch the world. Text-only embeddings keep the company of words, while multimodal embeddings add the company of the senses. Whether the result is one meaning seen through four channels, or four meanings that merely happen to be close, is a question the book returns to along the way. Chapters report partial answers where they find them, @sec-ch-meaning-across-senses gives its own, and the Epilogue collects them. The test is demanding: a shared space may keep what the four signals have in common and lose what is specific to each, and the way in which it loses it is part of the answer.

### The Critical Literacy Test {.idea}

<!-- Provisional (author, 2026-11-12): name, kinds of question and criteria are a first draft, and what the test is applied to (a single vector, a set of vectors, a model that reads the text) is undecided. The universal translator, a third thought experiment, lives in the Epilogue (idea 15). -->

The dog test varies the channel: one concept, several senses. A second question varies the scale. A word, a phrase, a paragraph, a section, a chapter and a whole book can each be placed in a space, but a book is not a word-like point. It is parts of several sizes, an order of prerequisites, and an argument that has to hold together and agree with the world. The *critical literacy test* asks whether the representation of a text, at each of those levels, supports what a good reader does with it: regenerate the text, to the fidelity the level allows, and answer questions about it, not only about what it states directly but about its consequences, its logical implications, and the places where two passages contradict each other.

Four kinds of question separate what a representation keeps. *Granularity*: how much of the detail survives at each level, which is Shannon's rate against distortion. *Dependency*: what must be known before a section can be read, an order of definitions that is a graph and not a tree. *Internal consistency*: whether the parts agree with each other and each claim follows from what came before. The verdict has three values and not two: a claim is entailed by the ground truth and the common sense assumed, or refuted (its negation is entailed), or undetermined (neither follows). Falsehood is therefore something derived by reasoning, not the absence of truth, and the test must tell it from ignorance: a representation that scores a claim as implausible has not shown it false. *External consistency*: whether the claims agree with sources outside the book that are known to be right. The aim is that each kind has a counterpart in the reading and reasoning tests already given to people and to models, so that the test can be scored. The hardest case, and the best testbed, is a deep mathematical subject, where a formal library gives the dependency graph and a proof checker confirms that a formal claim follows from earlier ones, or that its negation does, once the text has been translated into formal statements. When the checker can do neither, the claim is independent of what came before, which is ignorance and not falsehood.

The question is not whether a language model can answer questions about a text it is shown: today's appear to do it well, and the interesting questions come after that. How reliably across a whole book, and with a contradiction planted in it? What must a bounded representation keep, and in how many bits, for the answers to survive without the text? And does a correct answer come from the representation, from re-reading the text, or from training that already contained it? Whether geometry alone can carry consistency, or whether something beside the space, a retrieval step or a verifier, has to check it, is open, and the book does not assume the answer. Chapters report partial answers where they find them, and the Epilogue collects them.

### The Geek's Compass: Navigating Thousands of Dimensions

High-dimensional spaces do not behave like our 3D intuitive world. In 1,000 dimensions, nearly all the volume of a ball concentrates in a thin outer shell, thinner as the dimension grows; random vectors are almost certainly close to orthogonal ($\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle \approx 0$); and traditional Euclidean distance metrics lose discriminative power without careful geometric regularization. The same strangeness is a resource: there is room for exponentially many nearly orthogonal directions, which is what lets a distributed representation hold far more concepts than it has dimensions.

Navigating this counter-intuitive landscape requires a toolkit that blends linear algebra, differential geometry, group theory, topology, and hyperdimensional algebras. This book is your compass for that journey.

## Disclaimer {#sec-disclaimer .unnumbered}

The mathematics presented in this book, and the historical arguments that connect it, are meant to last: Shannon's entropy, Rice's theorem, and concentration of measure will not change with the next model release. Descriptions of specific systems, software libraries, API interfaces, model sizes, and benchmark numbers, by contrast, are a snapshot of the state of artificial intelligence, geometric deep learning, and neurosymbolic computing as of 2026. They are written as dated history wherever possible, so that they remain true as a record of what was done even when they are no longer current.

All code examples, mathematical proofs, and architectural blueprints are provided for educational and research purposes. While derivations are presented with rigorous mathematical grounding, simplified toy implementations are designed for conceptual clarity rather than production deployment. The author and publisher assume no liability for errors, omissions, or damages resulting from the use of the information contained herein.

## Book Architecture & Master Roadmap {#sec-book-architecture-master-roadmap .unnumbered}

The book is one sequence of chapters, with no Parts for the time being. It begins with an introduction that says what cannot be had and what we would like to have from a technology of meaning, then a living summary of the properties that a space of meanings is expected to have, then one chapter for each of those properties, and it ends with the epilogue; the geometry of high dimensions is an appendix. Every property chapter has the same shape. It starts from what the philosophies of meaning say about the property and asks how far a vector with a distance can carry it; it states its scope, and where something escapes it, it names the property that takes over; each claim is an expectation written before an experiment, with a null and a judge; it closes with the technologies that exploit the property, and with a section that says what was found, what was achieved for the representation of meaning and what is still out of reach. The methods that explored each property are told as history.

Three devices connect the chapters. The summary chapter keeps, for each property, what the literature and the chapters have shown, achieved, partial or not, together with a ledger of limits, each stated as a cost rather than an impossibility, and the property chapters take them up one by one. The *Next:* line of the roadmap is the short form of the last section of a chapter. And the tests of the introduction, the dog test, the critical literacy test, the universal translator and the alien technology test, ask what the structure at hand does for a concept that arrives through several senses, for a text that has to be read at several scales, for two languages with no dictionary, and for a system we did not build. They are not assigned to chapters: any chapter may bring a partial answer and says so in its closing section, and the Epilogue collects them.

Each chapter below carries a status tag, mirrored in the chapter's own file. *Definitive*: the chapter should exist, and what is already written in it is settled. *Provisional*: it probably exists, but its shape or its place is not settled. *Idea*: a question, not yet a decision; it is here so that we can see what the book might become, and it may be reshaped, merged, moved or dropped (dropped ideas are kept, with the reason, outside the book).

<!-- OPEN: the chapters are decided on arrival, from what the previous ones found: continue, reshape, merge or drop. Candidates for a merge: meaning_as_path with meaning_as_generation (both are travel through the space, over known and over unknown territory), and the two halves of meaning_as_arrangement (what survives a change of coordinates, and comparing two spaces). The technology chapters of the earlier plan (the anatomy of embedding spaces, generative spaces, contextual vectors, vector databases, geodesics, graphs, topology, complex numbers, hyperdimensional computing, neuro-symbolic integration, optimal transport, multimodal embeddings) are kept in embedding-technologies-stubs/ and each property chapter salvages from them what it needs. The order of the property chapters follows what each needs from the one before; context may belong earlier. * **@sec-ch-symbols-without-interior: Symbols Without Interior.** *(definitive)* Shannon separated the bit from meaning, and Chomsky's staircase adds memory for structure but never an interior to the symbols. A table of one-hot symbols puts every pair at the same distance, and Rice's theorem puts exact meaning out of reach even for programs, so similarity must be graded. *Next:* given that exact meaning is out of reach, what would we like to have from a technology of meaning?
* **@sec-ch-tests-of-meaning: The Tests of Meaning.** *(provisional)* The thought experiments of the Prologue and the Epilogue in one place and one format: the dog test (channels), the critical literacy test (scales), the universal translator (languages) and the alien technology test (systems). Each has a question, what it varies, who can judge, and a ladder of rungs, and a scorecard that later chapters fill when they reach a rung. The tests are not assigned to chapters. *Next:* what a space of meanings is expected to have, and what the literature says about each property.
* **@sec-ch-properties-of-meaning: The Properties of Meaning as Geometry.** *(provisional)* The living summary of the book. For each property of a space of meanings, in the plain language of distance and direction, what the literature and the chapters have shown (achieved, partial or not), what the sceptics found, and which chapter earns it; it grows and shrinks as the chapters are written, and the ledger of limits of the earlier plan is one of its sources. *Next:* the first property, nearness.
* **@sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness: Meaning as Likeness: What a Distance Can Carry.** *(idea)* What would likeness of meaning have to be, according to the philosophical accounts (Frege's idea, sense and reference, use and company, family resemblance, holism, Tversky's axioms, reference, indexicals, truth), and which of them can a vector with a distance carry? The accounts are turned into eighteen questions that a space can pass or fail. Twelve are tried in the chapter: whether neighbours look alike, whether nearness follows similarity, relatedness or association, whether it survives a change of loss, whether nearness is built in or emergent, what a raw cosine hides, whether likeness is a distance (Tversky's three axioms), where near is not alike, and how much of it survives another seed, algorithm or text. Six are handed on, to the chapters on arrangement, context, truth, regions, senses and difference. A nearness that is built in is a building block, and only the nearness that appears where it was not trained is a finding about meaning. *Next:* opposites and negations are near without being alike, so how is a difference built?
* **@sec-ch-meaning-as-difference: Meaning as Difference: Opposition, Relation and Negation.** *(idea)* The step from one meaning to another is itself meaningful. Meaning as a system of differences, opposition and negation (an antonym is near), analogy as an offset and its sceptics, relations as translations, rotations and bilinear forms (knowledge-graph embeddings told as a sequence in which each model fixes a pattern the previous one could not express), and what a single dot product cannot say (negation, conjunction). *Next:* a difference taken repeatedly in the same sense is a direction.
* **@sec-ch-meaning-as-direction: Meaning as Direction: Qualities You Can Move Along.** *(idea)* Qualities as dimensions of a space of meaning (Osgood's semantic differential, Gärdenfors), the linear representation hypothesis, features as directions and their superposition, sparse dictionaries, probing and steering, and the sceptics (a direction that can be read may not be a direction that is used). *Next:* a direction is one quality; a concept has extent.
* **@sec-ch-meaning-as-region: Meaning as Region: Concepts, Hierarchies and Subspaces.** *(idea)* A concept is a region and not a point: prototypes and family resemblance, balls, boxes, cones and subspaces, hyperbolic space where trees embed with low distortion, and negation as the orthogonal complement of a subspace. Each shape is kept only if it beats a point of the same size on a stated judge. *Next:* regions are static; events change.
* **@sec-ch-meaning-as-path: Meaning as Path: Events, Time and Travel Through Known Territory.** *(idea)* A static thing is a point and an event is a curve. Tangent spaces, geodesics and curvature, parallel transport (how a relation is carried from one place to another), time and motion, and travel between points that the data already hold. Travel beyond the data is the subject of the chapter on generation. *Next:* a path joins whole meanings; how are parts joined into a whole?
* **@sec-ch-meaning-as-composition: Meaning as Composition: How Parts Make a Whole.** *(idea)* Fodor and Pylyshyn's systematicity challenge (does a space tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog"?), binding and bundling, tensor product representations and hyperdimensional computing with their capacity bounds, logic tensor networks, and emergent symbolic structure. *Next:* a whole can be a phrase, a chunk or a text; what happens to a vector as it grows?
* **@sec-ch-meaning-across-scales: Meaning Across Scales: Words, Phrases, Chunks and Texts.** *(idea)* What is the representation of a word, a phrase, a sentence, a chunk, a document? What a vector of fixed size can hold as the text it stands for grows, pooled vectors against one vector per token (late interaction), chunking, and the critical literacy test (a text read at several scales). *Next:* the text is one sense; the dog arrives through several.
* **@sec-ch-meaning-across-senses: Meaning Across Senses: Many Views, One Space.** *(idea)* The grounding problem and the dog test, meaning as what views share, contrastive alignment around one hub, what a shared space loses, the modality gap, motion and time, prediction in latent space, and whether the senses converge. Two questions of its own: does a second sense improve the representation of meaning itself, and what else does it improve? Text is a second-hand trace of what bodies with several senses saw, so the expected answer is partial redundancy with a residue, and the chapter measures the residue. *Next:* two spaces trained on different data say the same only up to a change of coordinates.
* **@sec-ch-meaning-as-arrangement: Meaning as Arrangement: What Survives a Change of Coordinates.** *(idea)* The coordinates mean nothing and only the arrangement is real: gauge freedom, the symmetries a training objective leaves and the ones it breaks, relative representations, comparing two spaces (Procrustes, optimal transport, alignment with no pairs), Quine's indeterminacy of translation and the universal translator, and the shape of a representation (persistent homology, the manifold hypothesis). *Next:* so far a word has one place; its meaning changes with its situation.
* **@sec-ch-meaning-in-context: Meaning in Context: One Word, Many Vectors.** *(idea)* Harris, Firth and Kaplan on the dependence of meaning on its situation, polysemy and disambiguation, attention as similarity-weighted retrieval, what is near at each layer of a model, and reasoning written in text or kept in the space. *Next:* a vector that fits its context still says nothing about whether it is true.
* **@sec-ch-meaning-and-truth: Meaning and Truth: Reference, Checking and Hallucination.** *(idea)* A sense is not a truth value (Frege), a name is tied to its bearer (Kripke and Putnam), and "true" may be redundant (Ramsey). What a text-only space can reach, hallucination as plausible without being true, the ways to check (retrieval against sources and the vector indexes, exact and approximate, that search them, internal consistency, proofs, knowledge graphs), truth directions, reaching "false" and keeping it apart from "unknown", and logics with more than two verdicts. *Next:* a space that says what is plausible can also make it.
* **@sec-ch-meaning-as-generation: Meaning as Generation: Producing and Growing Meaning.** *(idea)* Meaning is not only read but made: decoding a point into an object, extrapolation beyond the data (travel over unknown territory, where nothing has fixed a metric), the latent spaces of variational, diffusion and autoregressive models, plausibility against truth, creativity as exploring or transforming a conceptual space, and the discovery of new regions. *Next:* the Epilogue collects what the tests found and asks what lies beyond.

* **Epilogue: An Algebra of Thought.** *(idea)* A box of ideas about meaning that no current technology satisfies. Each section states an idea, the tradition that reached it first (philosophy of meaning, linguistics and Chomsky's argument with statistics, biology, mathematics, logic and the limits of knowledge, decision under uncertainty, fallacy and bias, translation, the traditions of India and China on the limits of saying), and what the technologies of the book lack for it. It is reviewed once the property chapters are written, and a section whose idea a chapter carries goes there. The earlier sketch is kept in `notes/epilogue_sketch.qmd`.
* **@sec-ch-curse-of-dimensionality: Appendix: Why Vectors Work, the Blessing (and Curse) of Dimensionality.** *(provisional)* High dimensions break our intuition and are also what makes the idea possible: volume sits in a thin shell, random vectors are nearly orthogonal, distances concentrate, and yet there is room for exponentially many nearly orthogonal directions. Learning there needs structure, which real data supplies (the manifold hypothesis). The chapters on nearness and composition point here.

## Mathematical Notation & Conventions {#sec-mathematical-notation-conventions .unnumbered}

Throughout this book, we adopt standard mathematical notation:

* **Scalars**: Lowercase italic letters ($x, y, \alpha, \lambda, \tau$).
* **Vectors**: Lowercase bold letters ($\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{v}, \boldsymbol{\mu}$). Vectors are column vectors in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^D$ unless specified otherwise. A row of a matrix is written as a column vector when it is used alone: $\mathbf{e}_w$ is the $w$-th row of the embedding matrix $\mathbf{E}$. The one-hot vector of the $j$-th symbol is $\mathbf{o}_j$, so the lookup of a table is $\mathbf{E}^\top \mathbf{o}_j = \mathbf{e}_j$.
* **Matrices**: Uppercase bold letters ($\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{\Sigma}, \mathbf{U}$).
* **Manifolds & Sets**: Calligraphic letters ($\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{S}, \mathbb{S}^{D-1}$). A vocabulary is $\mathcal{V}$, with $|\mathcal{V}|$ symbols.
* **Dimensions**: $D$ is the dimension of the ambient space, of the data or of a space considered on its own (for a vocabulary, $D = |\mathcal{V}|$ for one-hot vectors). $d$ is the dimension of a learned or reduced representation (an embedding, a rank, a subspace), with $d \le D$, and $d_{\text{int}}$ is the intrinsic dimension of the data.
* **Information**: $P$ and $Q$ are probability distributions, $H$ is entropy, $I$ is mutual information and $\mathrm{PMI}$ is pointwise mutual information. Logarithms are base 2 (bits), except where training uses $\ln$ (nats), which is stated.
* **Inner Products**: $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^D u_i v_i$.
* **Norms**: Euclidean $L_2$ norm $\|\mathbf{x}\|_2 = \sqrt{\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x}}$; $L_p$ norm $\|\mathbf{x}\|_p = (\sum_i |x_i|^p)^{1/p}$.
* **Cosine Similarity**: $\cos(\theta) = \frac{\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|_2 \|\mathbf{v}\|_2}$. On the unit hypersphere $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ of a $d$-dimensional embedding, $\cos(\theta) = \mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{v}$.
* **Networks**: A network maps an input $\mathbf{x}$ to a code $\mathbf{z} = f(\mathbf{x})$ (the encoder $f$), and a decoder $g$ maps the code back, $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = g(\mathbf{z})$. The $\ell$-th layer computes $\mathbf{p}_\ell = \mathbf{W}_\ell \mathbf{a}_{\ell-1} + \mathbf{b}_\ell$ and $\mathbf{a}_\ell = \varphi_\ell(\mathbf{p}_\ell)$, with $\mathbf{a}_0 = \mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{W}_\ell$ of shape (outputs $\times$ inputs), so a weight matrix multiplies a column vector from the left. The error signal of the layer is $\boldsymbol{\delta}_\ell = \partial L / \partial \mathbf{p}_\ell$. A table of embeddings $\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times d}$ has one row per symbol, so a lookup is the layer with weight matrix $\mathbf{E}^\top$.
* **Scoring roles**: For a pair of things to be compared, $\mathbf{e}$ is the vector of the thing looked at (an anchor) and $\mathbf{v}$ the vector of the candidate (a neighbour), so the score is $\langle \mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{v}_j \rangle$; when two encoders produce them they are $f_x$ and $f_y$.
* **Noise and batches**: $k$ is the number of noise neighbours (alternatives) that accompany each real pair. A contrastive batch has $k+1$ matched pairs, so that each positive has the $k$ others as alternatives.
* **Modalities**: A modality is indexed by $m$ (text, image, audio, video), with input space $\mathcal{X}_m$ and encoder $f_m : \mathcal{X}_m \to \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. A shared space is one in which $f_m(x_m)$ and $f_{m'}(x_{m'})$ are close whenever $x_m$ and $x_{m'}$ are views of the same thing.

## Code & Computational Environment {#sec-code-computational-environment .unnumbered}

All code examples in this book are executable Python scripts and Jupyter notebooks using the project virtual environment (`.venv`). 

```bash
# Activate the book environment
source .venv/bin/activate

# Build all book formats (PDF, HTML, EPUB)
make book
```

Figures and computational simulations are generated programmatically using standard scientific Python libraries: NumPy, SciPy, PyTorch, Matplotlib, and Scikit-learn.
